issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant deserved to be enlarged on bail.

facts: The appellant was accused of offenses related to six counterfeit currency notes of Rs. 500 each.
The appellant had already been incarcerated for two and a half years.
A counter affidavit filed by the State confirmed that the appellant had no prior criminal record (antecedents).
The trial was not expected to conclude in a reasonable amount of time.
law: The Court applied the well-settled legal principle that 'bail is rule and jail is an exception'.
application: The Court weighed the specific facts of the case against the general principle for granting bail. It considered the prolonged period of pre-trial detention (two and a half years), the appellant's lack of a criminal history, and the unlikelihood of a speedy trial.
Given these circumstances, the Court determined that continued incarceration was not justified.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant deserved to be enlarged on bail. It directed the Trial Court to release the appellant on appropriate terms and conditions until the conclusion of the trial.

issue.issue_text: Whether it is appropriate for the High Court to fix a time-bound schedule for the conclusion of trials.

facts: The Supreme Court observed a trend where various High Courts, while rejecting bail applications, were routinely fixing a time-bound schedule for the conclusion of trials in the lower courts.
law: The Court cited a Constitution Bench decision in 'High Court Bar Association, Allahabad vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.', which held in paragraph 47.3 that constitutional courts should ordinarily refrain from fixing time-bound schedules for cases pending in other courts and should only do so in exceptional circumstances.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that this routine practice by High Courts has several negative consequences. Firstly, it adversely affects the functioning of Trial Courts, which may have older cases of the same category pending. It creates an unfair system where a person who files a case in a higher court gets an "out of turn hearing" for their trial, disrupting the prioritization that should be left to the Trial Courts.

Secondly, the Court noted that such orders are often difficult to implement and give false hope to litigants. It suggested that these directions are sometimes given to provide some "satisfaction" to an accused whose bail has been rejected.

The Court clarified that if an accused is entitled to relief due to long incarceration without trial progress, the appropriate remedy is to grant bail, stating that the "option of expediating trial is not the solution."
The Court criticized the High Courts for routinely issuing these directions without considering the established law that this power should only be used in "exceptional circumstances."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that it is not appropriate for High Courts to routinely fix a time-bound schedule for the conclusion of trials. This practice should be reserved only for exceptional circumstances, as it disrupts the functioning of trial courts, creates an unfair prioritization of cases, and offers a false sense of hope. The Court held that the decision of when to prioritize cases should be left to the concerned trial courts.

cases.case_name: High Court Bar Association, Allahabad v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
cases.principle: Constitutional courts, in the ordinary course, should refrain from fixing a time-bound schedule for the disposal of cases pending before any other courts and may issue such directions only in exceptional circumstances.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Constitutional courts, in the ordinary course, should refrain from fixing a time-bound schedule for the disposal of cases pending before any other courts and may only issue such directions in exceptional circumstances, as the prioritization of cases is best left to the decision of the courts where the cases are pending.
obiter: Directions for time-bound disposal of cases adversely affect the functioning of the Trial Courts, as there may be older cases of the same category pending.
Every court has cases that require expeditious disposal for various reasons, such as statutory requirements, long incarceration, or the age of the accused.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that if an accused is entitled to bail on the ground of long incarceration without the trial making any progress, the Court must grant bail. The alternative of expediting the trial is not the proper solution. Furthermore, the Court held that High Courts are routinely and improperly fixing time-bound schedules for the conclusion of trials, which is contrary to the law laid down by a Constitution Bench that such directions should only be issued in exceptional circumstances.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied the precedent from the Constitution Bench decision in ‘High Court Bar Association, Allahabad vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.’, specifically paragraph 47.3, which states: 'Constitutional courts, in the ordinary course, should refrain from fixing a time-bound schedule for the disposal of cases pending before any other courts. Constitutional courts may issue directions for the time-bound disposal of cases only in exceptional circumstances.'
policy_considerations: Directions for time-bound trials adversely affect the functioning of Trial Courts, as there may be older cases of the same category pending.
An individual who files a case in a Constitutional Court should not get an out-of-turn hearing for their trial at the expense of other pending cases.
Orders fixing a time-bound schedule for trials are difficult for lower courts to implement.
Such orders give a false hope to litigants.
Prioritising the disposal of cases should be best left to the decision of the courts where the cases are pending.
